summary:
ASTRA-AI is a dashboard where an astronaut can check their own health in a few seconds. A simulator writes vitals every 5 seconds for two crew members: heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature, stress and sleep. Each vital sits on a threshold bar, and a Gemini-based agent turns the latest values into one status (normal, caution or alert), a short explanation and one thing to do. The user can rotate a 3D body, click a zone such as the lungs or the spine, and read tips for it. An optional 8-question test updates stress and fatigue. The interface works in English and Russian.

Problems like sleep debt build up slowly and are easy to miss in raw numbers, so we show trends and a plain verdict instead. The data is simulated, the tool only suggests and never decides, and the whole project was written with Claude and Gemini.
details:
ASTRA-AI is a dashboard for monitoring the health of astronauts on a long mission. It is a decision-support tool: it does not diagnose anything, and all thresholds are for demonstration, not clinical norms.

How it works. Three parts share one file, state.json. A simulator writes telemetry for two crew members (ASTRO-01 and ASTRO-02) every 5 seconds: heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, stress and sleep. A backend built with LangGraph reads that file, sends the latest values to Google Gemini, and writes the answer back: a status (normal, caution or alert), a short explanation and one thing to do. The Streamlit interface reads the same file.

What the user sees. The interface has five tabs: mission overview, AI and risks, vitals and trends, body zones, and well-being. The overview shows each crew member's status and every vital on a threshold bar. The trends tab has charts of recent values and sleep over the last days. On the body zones tab the user rotates a 3D body and clicks a zone (heart and vessels, lungs, muscles, lower back and spine and others) to read a short explanation and tips; the selected zone is passed to the AI as context for the next analysis. An optional 8-question well-being test updates stress and fatigue; without it these values come from the simulator, and the interface says so. The built-in tips do not depend on the AI. Everything works in English and Russian.

Why we made it this way. We wanted one screen where an astronaut can see in a few seconds whether something is off and what to do about it, instead of reading a table of numbers. Hazard and risk names (space radiation, isolation and confinement, inadequate sleep and irregular schedules, and others) follow the NASA Human Research Program pages and are shown as context for the selected zone. We do not use NASA data: all telemetry is simulated.

Tools. Python, Streamlit, Altair, pandas, LangGraph, the Google Gemini API, VS Code. The 3D body model is drawn in raw WebGL inside an iframe, with no external 3D libraries, models, textures or CDN scripts. The whole project, including all of the code, was written with AI assistance: Claude and Gemini.

What we took into account. The tool only suggests and never decides, because an AI verdict can be wrong. We say clearly that the data is simulated and which parts use AI. The well-being test is optional and takes about a minute.

Safety and limits. The AI cannot raise a red alert on its own: a red status is possible only if the built-in rules also give red, and if the rules say red, the verdict is red. If the AI text mentions drugs, doses or medical procedures, it is replaced by a neutral text. If Gemini is unavailable or the daily request limit of the free tier is reached, the app switches to the built-in rules. The thresholds are for demonstration, not clinical norms, and the zone descriptions and tips are not verified by a physician. Gemini is a cloud model and would not work beyond Earth orbit, so a real mission would need a local model; we have not implemented one yet. Next we plan to add an offline mode with a local model through Ollama.
